standard.title: Simple sentences
standard.description: understand that a simple sentence consists of a single independent clause representing a single event or idea
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can recognise that sentences are key units for expressing ideas (AC9EFLA05). They have not yet understood the internal structure of a simple sentence — that it consists of a single independent clause with a process (verb), participants (noun groups) and optional circumstances (adverbs).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand that a simple sentence is a single independent clause representing one event or idea, containing a process, participants and optional circumstances.

nodes.label: A sentence expresses one event or idea
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that a sentence expresses one complete event or idea and recognise when a sentence is complete.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify whether a given group of words is a complete sentence (expresses a complete event or idea) or is incomplete.
nodes.typical_width: Identify complete sentences and explain what makes them complete — they express a whole event or idea. Distinguish complete sentences from fragments and from sequences of multiple events.
wider: Sort a set of word groups into complete sentences and fragments, explaining the decision for each
Find examples of single-event sentences in a familiar picture book and discuss what each one expresses
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably identify a complete sentence cannot identify the participant and process structure in N2 — the completeness concept is definitionally prior to analysis of what a complete sentence contains.

response_modes.reason: Recognising a complete sentence requires repeated exposure to both examples and non-examples. Students need practice judging completeness across varied sentence types before moving to internal structure.

success_criteria: Student correctly identifies at least three complete sentences in a mixed set
Student explains why a given fragment is not a complete sentence

nodes.label: Sentences have participants and processes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the participant (who or what) and the process (what is happening) in a simple sentence.
nodes.minimum_width: In a given simple sentence, identify who or what is involved and what is happening.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the participant (noun group) and process (verb) in simple sentences, and explain what each contributes to the sentence's meaning — who/what is doing or being something, and what that doing or being is.
wider: Explore sentences with more than one participant (e.g. 'The cat chased the mouse') and identify both participants and the process
Investigate how changing the participant or process changes the meaning of a sentence

response_modes.reason: Students often focus on identifying the 'doing word' without grasping that participant and process work together as a minimum sentence unit. Varied sentence examples — different participant types, different verb types — help establish the interdependence of these elements.

success_criteria: Student correctly identifies the participant and process in at least three simple sentences
Student explains what the participant and process each contribute to the meaning

nodes.label: Circumstances add detail
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify circumstantial detail (when, where, how) in simple sentences and explain that these details are optional additions to the core event.
nodes.minimum_width: In a given sentence, identify one circumstantial detail (where, when or how) and confirm the sentence would still make sense without it.
nodes.typical_width: Identify circumstantial details (adverb groups/phrases answering when, where, how) in simple sentences, and understand that these extend the sentence without creating a new independent clause.
wider: Construct simple sentences that express the same core event with and without circumstances, discussing how meaning changes
Sort circumstantial details by type (when/where/how) across a range of simple sentences
success_criteria: Student identifies a circumstantial detail in a sentence and names what it answers (when/where/how)
Student confirms the sentence's core event is still expressed without the circumstance

nodes.label: The clause as a unit
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that a simple sentence is a single independent clause — one complete event or idea expressed with a participant, process and optional circumstances.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain that a simple sentence contains one clause representing one event, with a who/what, a doing/being, and optional details.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the structure of a simple sentence as a single independent clause, identifying its key elements (participant, process, optional circumstances) and understanding that adding circumstances does not create a new clause.
wider: Identify simple sentences and multi-clause sentences in a short text and discuss the difference
Examine how authors use simple sentences for effect — pace, clarity, emphasis — in narrative and informative texts

response_modes.reason: This final node integrates participant, process and circumstance into the unified concept of the independent clause — the core schema students need before Year 2 work on compound sentences.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Examining how authors deliberately choose simple sentences for stylistic effect gives advancing students a genuine analytical task that bridges grammar and literary response.
success_criteria: Student explains, in their own words, what makes a sentence a 'simple sentence'
Student correctly identifies participant, process and any circumstances in a new example sentence
